## Column mapping onto Verify's POST /v1.0/applications body:
##   name             -> name  (the application's display name in the console)
##   role             -> which demo job this client does; drives the defaults
##                       below. One of: mint | exchange | audience | agent
##   ropc             -> providers.oidc.properties.grantTypes.ropc
##   client_creds     -> providers.oidc.properties.grantTypes.clientCredentials
##   token_exchange   -> providers.oidc.properties.grantTypes.tokenExchange
##   audiences        -> providers.oidc.token.audiences        (pipe-separated)
##   claims           -> providers.oidc.token.attributeMappings (pipe-separated;
##                       each becomes a CELx mapper — see import-verify-clients.sh)
##   pdv_id_key       -> where the generated client_id is written back into
##   pdv_secret_key      post_deploy_variables.json (blank = do not write back)
## Grant-type cells are true/false and become the QUOTED strings Verify requires.
## An empty audiences/claims cell means "none".
## `manager` is mapped from a RELATIONSHIP
## The other four claims are sets read out of custom attributes through a CELx
## mapper that returns getCustomValues() as-is — the trailing "" pad these used to
## carry is gone

column1: ## import-verify-clients.sh). `manager` is different in kind: it is the SCIM
## EnterpriseUser manager reference
##   statements:
##     - context: manager := user.getManager()
##     - return: context.manager.userName
## — yielding the scalar string "alice". policy-verify-opa.yaml consumes it as
## require_approval(from: claim.manager) and hands it to CIBA as the login_hint
## naming the approver
## from its RELATIONSHIP_CLAIMS list; listing the claim here is enough.
## It is listed on BOTH real clients on purpose. The mint client is where bob's
## token gets it; the exchange client needs it as well
## at the RFC 8693 exchange and the gateway — the thing that actually evaluates
## require_approval — never sees it.
## Why four rows when Verify only needs two clients
## The Keycloak realm has four clients. Only two of them are real OAuth clients
## on Verify:
##   hr-copilot     mints user + client tokens (ROPC + client_credentials)
##   praxis-gateway performs the RFC 8693 exchange
## They must stay distinct: Verify refuses to let a client exchange its own
## tokens (CSIAQ5207E)
column2: the same split the realm export already has.

column1: ## github-api and workday-api are NOT clients on Verify — they are audience
## STRINGS in the exchange client's `audiences` list (see delta V1 in
## docs/brainstorms/2026-08-31-ibm-verify-idp-requirements.md). They are
## registered here as `role=audience` so this file mirrors the realm export
## 1:1 and the console shows the same four names a viewer sees in Keycloak.
## Three things registering them does NOT do:
##   - it does not make Verify honor a requested `audience` (delta V1: Verify
##     stamps the exchanging client's fixed list and accepts unregistered
##     audiences silently);
##   - it does not reproduce Keycloak's per-audience `gh-permissions-as-scope`
##     mapper

column1: ## role=agent — the non-human principal (scenario 14)
## An IBM Verify Agent Identity: a governed principal that acts as ITSELF
## no human in the loop. It mints with client_credentials and calls search_repos
## on its own authority.
## Three things make it unlike the rows above:
##   - It carries NO claims. A client_credentials token cannot carry custom
##     claims on this tenant — attribute mappers read user attributes
##     client-credentials grant has no user. Verified four ways against
##     praxis-2; see docs/brainstorms/2026-10-20-verify-agent-identity-requirements.md
##     (finding E3). The agent's authority is its SCOPE
##   - Its OWN client needs no application entitlement: nothing authenticates
##     TO the agent's client. But it does force a change on the EXCHANGE
##     client. Application entitlement is checked against the exchange
##     SUBJECT
